title: Physics and Measurement
notes: Introduction to Physics and Quantities
Physics is the branch of science that deals with natural phenomena at all scales, from subatomic particles to the entire universe. It deals with matter, energy, and the interactions between them.
The word Science originates from the Latin verb Scientia, meaning 'to know', representing systematically organized knowledge built on observations and experiments.

The term Physics is derived from the Greek word Physika, which means 'nature'. In Sanskrit, it is called Bhautika, which refers to the physical world, and an expert in this field is called a physicist.
Mathematics is considered the language of the universe, and physics heavily utilizes it as a powerful tool to describe basic laws of nature.
Branches of Mechanics
Mechanics is the branch of physics dealing with bodies either at rest or in motion.

• Statics: The branch of mechanics that deals with a body at rest.
  • Kinetics: The branch of mechanics that deals with a body in motion. It is further sub-divided into:
    • Kinematics: Derived from the Greek word kinema (meaning motion), it describes how objects move without taking into account the causes of that motion.
    • Dynamics: Derived from the Greek word dynamis (meaning power), it deals with why objects move as they do, acting as the general science of motion.
Particle vs. Body

• Particle (Point Object): A mathematical model of a mass point where its size (dimension) is negligible compared to another body or the distance involved (e.g., a football compared to a house).
  • Body: An object that possesses a certain size, mass, and volume.
Physical Quantities
Physical quantities are measurable quantities in terms of which the laws of physics are expressed. All physical quantities possess both a magnitude and a unit: Physical Quantity = Magnitude * Unit.
The numerical value N depends on the choice of unit U; a larger unit size results in a smaller numerical value, and vice versa. N is always positive.
Types of Physical Quantities

• Fundamental (Basic) Quantity: Quantities that do not depend on any other quantities. There are seven basic quantities: length, mass, time (Mechanics); illuminating power/luminous intensity (Optics); temperature (Heat); electric current (Electricity); and amount of chemical substance (Nuclear Physics). Sub-fundamental quantities include plane angle and solid angle.
  • Derived Quantity: Quantities obtained from fundamental quantities (e.g., Area, Density, Speed).
Measurement in Physics

Measurement is the process of comparing an unknown quantity with a known constant unit, determining the quantity of something. To measure a physical quantity, two things must be known: Unit and Numerical Value.

Principle of Measurement: The product of magnitude and unit always remains constant regardless of the system of units used (N * U = Constant or N1 * U1 = N2 * U2). Magnitude is inversely proportional to the scale of the unit.
Measurement provides objective observations identical for everyone. As stated by Lord Kelvin, knowledge is truly satisfactory only when expressed in numbers; measurement is the root of science.
Units of a Physical Quantity

A unit is a standard chosen quantity in terms of which a physical quantity is measured. It must be well-defined, convenient, easily reproducible, and independent of time, place, or physical conditions.
Fundamental Unit: A unit used to measure a fundamental quantity (e.g., kilogram, gram, meter).
Unit Classifications

• Non-Standard Units: Obscure units based on historical standards (e.g., firkin for volume, eon for time).
  • Hybrid Units: Combining units from two different measurement systems for a single physical quantity (e.g., ohm centimeter for resistivity).
Key Conversions

• 1 Fermi (femtometer): 10^-15 m (used for nuclear sizes)
  • 1 Angstrom: 10^-10 m
  • 1 Astronomical Unit (AU): 1.5 * 10^11 m
  • 1 Light Year: 9.5 * 10^15 m
  • 1 Parsec: 3.26 light years (3.08 * 10^16 m; largest practical unit of distance used for stars/galaxies)
  • 1 Litre: 10^-3 m^3
Dimensions of a Physical Quantity
The concept was introduced clearly by Joseph Fourier in 1822, though the foundational principle was known to Isaac Newton in 1686.
Definition: The dimensions of a physical quantity are the powers, indices, or exponents to which the base fundamental quantities must be raised to represent that quantity.
Base Representation: In mechanics, the fundamental quantities are represented by capital letters enclosed in square brackets, including Mass as M, Length as L, and Time as T.

Base Dimensional Symbols for all seven fundamental quantities: Length as L, Mass as M, Time as T, Temperature as K or theta, Electric Current as A or I, Amount of Substance as N, and Luminous Intensity as J.

• Dimensional Formula: An expression showing how and which basic quantities are involved in a derived physical quantity, usually written inside square brackets, such as Force equaling MLT to the power of -2.
  • Dimensional Equation: An equation obtained by equating a physical quantity with its dimensional formula.
  • Dimension vs. Unit: They are related but distinct. A physical quantity has only one unique dimensional formula, but its unit can differ across systems such as SI versus CGS.
  • Constants & Variables: Quantities can be dimensional constants like the universal gravitational constant G, dimensionless constants like pi, dimensional variables, and dimensionless variables.

1.3 Physical Quantity
• Definition: A measurable quantity in terms of which the laws of physics are expressed is called a physical quantity (e.g., length, mass, time, area, density, volume, pressure).
• Mathematical Expression: All physical quantities possess both a magnitude and a unit. This is expressed mathematically as:
physical quantity = Magnitude × unit = Numerical value (N) × Unit (U)
• Value Relationship: The numerical value N depends on the choice of unit U. A larger unit size results in a smaller numerical value, and vice versa. N is always positive.
Types of Physical Quantity
Physical quantities are broadly divided into two major types:

• Fundamental (Basic) Quantity: A quantity that does not depend on any other quantities. There are only seven basic quantities in physics: length, mass, and time (Mechanics); illuminating power (Optics); temperature (Heat); electric current (Electricity); and amount of chemical substance (Nuclear Physics). There are also two sub-fundamental quantities: plane angle and solid angle.
• Derived Quantity: A quantity that is obtained from fundamental quantities is called a derived quantity or compound quantity. Examples include:
- Area: Length × Breadth = length × length
- Density: mass/volume = mass/length³
- Speed: Distance/time = length/time
1.4 Measurement in Physics
• Definition: The process of comparing an unknown quantity with a known constant unit is called measurement. In general, it means determining the quantity of something.
• Requirements: To measure a physical quantity, two things must be known:
- Unit: The standard of measurement.
- Numerical Value: The number of times that unit is contained within the physical quantity (magnitude).
• Principle of Measurement: The product of magnitude and unit always remains constant regardless of the system of units used:
N × U = Constant or N₁ × U₁ = N₂ × U₂
Therefore, the magnitude (N) is inversely proportional to the scale of the unit (U).
Need for Measurement
Measurement provides objective observations that are identical for everyone.

• Scientific Precision: As stated by Lord Kelvin, knowledge is truly satisfactory only when expressed in numbers. A quantity that cannot be measured has no place in physics. Measurement is the root of science.
1.5 Unit of a Physical Quantity

• Definition: A standard chosen quantity in terms of which a physical quantity is measured is called a unit. It must be well-defined, convenient, easily reproducible, and independent of time, place, or physical conditions.
• Fundamental Unit: A unit used to measure a fundamental quantity is called a fundamental unit (e.g., kilogram or gram for mass, meter for length).
• Reproducible & Invariant: They are easily reproduced and do not change over time.
Unit Classifications & Useful Units
• Non-Standard Units: Obscure units based on historical or non-microscopic standards (e.g., firkin for volume, eon = 10⁹ years for time).
• Hybrid Units: Combining units from two different measurement systems for a single physical quantity (e.g., ohm centimeter for resistivity).
• Key Distance & Volume Conversions:
- 1 fermi (femtometer): 10⁻¹⁵ m
- 1 Angstrom (Å): 10⁻¹⁰ m
- 1 Astronomical Unit (AU): 1.5 × 10¹¹ m
- 1 Light Year: 9.5 × 10¹⁵ m
- 1 Parsec: 3.26 light years
- 1 Litre: 10⁻³ m³
Answer to Stop to Think 1.3
Based on the "Some Useful Units" section on this page, the smallest and largest practical units of distance are:
• Smallest Practical Unit: Fermi (also called femtometer), which is equal to 10⁻¹⁵ m. It is typically used to measure nuclear sizes.
• Largest Practical Unit: Parsec, which equals 3.26 light years (approximately 3.08 × 10¹⁶ m). It is used to measure astronomical distances between stars and galaxies.

Section 1.1: Introduction to Physics and Quantities
• Physics Definition: Physics is the branch of science that deals with natural phenomena at all scales, from subatomic particles to the entire universe.

• Physical Quantities: To explain natural phenomena, we require laws of physics. These laws are expressed in terms of physical quantities such as force, velocity, and volume. Physics cannot be studied without physical quantities.
• Core Aim: The primary objective of this chapter is to describe these physical quantities and explain the need for their measurement.
Section 1.2: What is Physics?
• Origin of "Science": The word Science originates from the Latin verb Scientia, which means "to know". It represents systematically organized knowledge built on observations and experiments.
• Origin of "Physics": The term Physics is derived from the Greek word Physika (Φύσις), which means "nature".
• Sanskrit Equivalent: In Sanskrit, physics is called Bhautika, which refers to the physical world.
• The Expert: An expert who specializes in this field of science is called a physicist.
Definition of Physics & Its Relationship with Mathematics
• Physics & Matter: Physics is defined as the branch of science that deals with matter, energy, and the interactions between them.
• Language of Physics: Mathematics is considered the language of the universe, and physics heavily utilizes it as a powerful tool to describe basic laws of nature.
Branches of Mechanics
Mechanics is the branch of physics dealing with bodies either at rest or in motion. It is classified into the following hierarchies:
• Statics: The branch of mechanics that deals with a body at rest.
• Kinetics: The branch of mechanics that deals with a body in motion. Kinetics is further sub-divided into:
- Kinematics: Derived from the Greek word kinema (meaning motion). It describes how objects move without taking into account the causes of that motion.
- Dynamics: Derived from the Greek word dynamis (meaning power). It deals with why objects move as they do, acting as the general science of motion.
Particle vs. Body
• Particle (Point Object): A mathematical model of a mass point where its size (dimension) is negligible compared to another body or the distance involved (e.g., a football compared to a house).
• Body: An object that possesses a certain size, mass, and volume (e.g., the house itself in the previous comparison).
Need for Measurement

• Subjective vs. Objective: Before systematic measurement, observations relied on human senses and were subjective (varying from person to person). Measurement provides objective observations that are identical for everyone.

• Scientific Precision: As stated by Lord Kelvin, knowledge is truly satisfactory only when expressed in numbers. A quantity that cannot be measured has no place in physics. Measurement is the root of science.
1.5 Unit of a Physical Quantity

• Definition: A standard chosen quantity in terms of which a physical quantity is measured is called a unit. It must be well-defined, convenient, easily reproducible, and independent of time, place, or physical conditions.
• Fundamental Unit: A unit used to measure a fundamental quantity is called a fundamental unit (e.g., kilogram or gram for mass).
Environmental & Physical Conditions Affecting Measurement
Here are examples of environmental and physical conditions that can affect reference standards, materials, and scientific measurements:
• Humidity: The amount of moisture or water vapor present in the surrounding air.
• Altitude: The elevation above sea level, which directly alters atmospheric density.
• Magnetic field: External magnetic forces that can interfere with electronic instruments.
• Electric field: Ambient electrical charges or fields that influence sensitive calibrations.
• Mechanical stress: External forces, tension, or vibrations applied directly to an object.
• Light intensity: Exposure to surrounding radiation, solar energy, or illumination levels.
